5.3 Birch’s theorem

In Section 5.4, we prove two extensions to the following theorem.

Theorem 5.12 (Birch’s theorem).

Let H⊆ℝmH\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} be a linear subspace, and let α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. The relative interior of the polyhedron 𝒫=(p+H)∩ℝ≥0m\mathcal{P}=(p+H)\cap\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0} intersects the toric pencil Toricα⁡(H⟂)\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp}) at exactly one point.

Variants of Birch’s theorem appear across the mathematical sciences. In algebraic statistics, toric pencils appear as log-linear statistical models, and in this setting, Theorem 5.12 was first proved by Birch in 1963 [11]. In dynamical systems, in the setting of chemical reaction systems, the theorem was proved by Horn and Jackson [27, Lemma 4B].

In the setting of quasi-thermostatic chemical reaction systems (a class introduced by Horn and Jackson that includes complex-balanced systems and therefore deficiency zero systems as well [18, 27]), the toric pencil in Birch’s theorem is equal to the set of positive steady states. In that context, the toric pencil usually is written as {c∈ℝ>0m∣log⁡cα∈H⟂}\{c\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{m}\mid\log\frac{c}{\alpha}\in H^{\perp}\}, where α\alpha is a given steady state.

Theorem 5.12 prompts the following definition.

Definition 5.13.

Let H⊆ℝmH\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} be a subspace, and let α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. The α\alpha-Birch point of the polyhedron 𝒫=(p+H)∩ℝ≥0m\mathcal{P}=(p+H)\cap\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0} is the unique point in the intersection int⁡𝒫∩Toricα⁡(H⟂)\operatorname{int}\mathcal{P}\cap\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp}).

We refer to the Birch point when the choice of α\alpha and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is clear from context. Horn [25] conjectured that every Birch point of a complex-balanced system is a global attractor of the corresponding invariant polyhedron int⁡𝒫\operatorname{int}\mathcal{P} (Conjecture 4.3).

The following is a conventional form of Birch’s theorem in the setting of algebraic statistics, as stated in the book by Pachter and Sturmfels [37, Theorem 1.10].

Theorem 5.14 (Birch’s theorem, restated).

Fix a d×md\times m real matrix AA with columns denoted by a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m} and positive vectors α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. The image of the monomial map

fA,α:ℝ>0d\displaystyle f_{A,\alpha}:\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d} →ℝ>0m\displaystyle\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{m}
Θ\displaystyle\Theta ↦α∗(Θa1,…,Θam)\displaystyle\mapsto\alpha*(\Theta^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Theta^{a_{m}})

intersects the polyhedron 𝒫={q∈ℝ≥0m∣A​q=A​p}\mathcal{P}=\{q\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}\mid Aq=Ap\} in a single point.

Remark 5.15.

To see why Theorems 5.12 and 5.14 are equivalent, first observe that the two definitions of the polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P} coincide because H=ker⁡AH=\ker A. It remains to show that

fA,α​(ℝ>0d)=Toricα⁡(H⟂)={α∗θw∣θ∈ℝ>0​ and ​w∈H⟂}.\displaystyle f_{A,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d})=\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp})=\{\alpha*\theta^{w}\mid\theta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\text{ and }w\in H^{\perp}\}. (9)

Given a vector α∗(Θa1,…,Θam)\alpha*(\Theta^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Theta^{a_{m}}) in the image of fA,αf_{A,\alpha}, when θ=Θ1\theta=\Theta_{1} and

w=a⁡(1)+(logΘ1⁡(Θ2))​a​(2)+⋯+(logΘ1⁡(Θd))​a​(d),w=a(1)+\big(\log_{\Theta_{1}}(\Theta_{2})\big)a(2)+\cdots+\big(\log_{\Theta_{1}}(\Theta_{d})\big)a(d),

where a⁡(j)a(j) denotes the jjth row of AA, the point α∗(Θa1,…,Θam)=α∗θw\alpha*(\Theta^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Theta^{a_{m}})=\alpha*\theta^{w} lies in the set on the right-hand side of (9). Conversely, given α∗θw\alpha*\theta^{w} where θ>0\theta>0 and ww is a linear combination of the rows of AA: w=c1​a​(1)+⋯+cd​a​(d)w=c_{1}a(1)+\cdots+c_{d}a(d), then for Θ=(θc1,…,θcd)\Theta=\big(\theta^{c_{1}},\ldots,\theta^{c_{d}}\big), it follows that α∗θw=fA,α​(Θ)\alpha*\theta^{w}=f_{A,\alpha}(\Theta) lies in the image of the map fA,αf_{A,\alpha}. Thus (9) holds.

5.4 Extensions

We extend Birch’s theorem to the compactification [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m} of the nonnegative orthant ℝ≥0m\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}.

Theorem 5.16 (Birch’s theorem at infinity).

Fix a linear subspace H⊆ℝmH\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. The α\alpha-Birch point of the polyhedron 𝒫=(p+H)∩ℝ≥0m\mathcal{P}=(p+H)\cap\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0} is the unique point in the intersection

𝒫¯∩Toricα⁡(H⟂)¯,\displaystyle{\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\cap{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp})}}, (10)

where the two closures are taken in the compactification [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m}.

We call this theorem “Birch’s theorem at infinity” because we are studying the same intersection problem as in the original Birch’s theorem, but now the parameter θ\theta along toric rays is allowed to take the value +∞+\infty.

Proof.

The intersection (10) has just one point in ℝ>0m\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}, namely the α\alpha-Birch point of 𝒫\mathcal{P}; this follows from the usual Birch’s theorem (Theorem 5.12). Therefore, we need only prove the lack of boundary points x∗x^{*} in the intersection (10). To this end, let x∗∈Toricα⁡(H⟂)¯∩∂𝒫¯x^{*}\in{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp})}}\cap\partial{\overline{\mathcal{P}}} and choose a sequence x⁡(n)=α∗θ​(i)w⁡(i)→x∗x(n)=\alpha*\theta(i)^{w(i)}\to x^{*}, where θ⁡(i)→∞\theta(i)\to\infty and w⁡(i)∈H⟂∩Sm−1w(i)\in H^{\perp}\cap S^{m-1}. Taking a subsequence if necessary, assume that w⁡(n)w(n) converges to some u∈H⟂∩Sm−1u\in H^{\perp}\cap S^{m-1}. By Lemma 5.7, ∇gα​(x​(n))∥∇gα​(x⁡(n))∥=w⁡(n)→u\frac{\nabla g_{\alpha}(x(n))}{\lVert\nabla g_{\alpha}(x(n))\rVert}=w(n)\to u. By Lemma 5.10, the direction uu lies in the outer normal cone of [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m} at x∗x^{*}. Therefore the outer normal cone intersects H⟂H^{\perp} nontrivially, so by Lemma 5.11, the point x∗x^{*} does not lie in ∂𝒫¯\partial{\overline{\mathcal{P}}}. Thus the intersection (10) is empty. ∎

By Theorem 5.16, when w∈H⟂w\in H^{\perp} the toric ray Toricα⁡(w)\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(w) either intersects 𝒫¯{\overline{\mathcal{P}}} at the Birch point or does not approach 𝒫¯{\overline{\mathcal{P}}}, including its boundary. The following theorem considers toric rays where ww lies more generally in a neighborhood of H⟂H^{\perp} and states that these toric rays do not approach 𝒫¯{\overline{\mathcal{P}}} outside a compact neighborhood of the Birch point.

Theorem 5.17 (Perturbed Birch’s theorem).

Fix a linear subspace H⊆ℝmH\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and vectors α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. Let qq be the α\alpha-Birch point in the polyhedron 𝒫=(p+H)∩ℝ≥0m\mathcal{P}=(p+H)\cap\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0}, namely the unique point in the intersection int⁡(𝒫)∩Toricα⁡(H⟂)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\cap\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H^{\perp}). For every relatively open neighborhood 𝒪\mathcal{O} of qq in the relative interior of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the set H⟂∩Sm−1H^{\perp}\cap S^{m-1} of unit directions along H⟂H^{\perp} has a relatively open neighborhood NN in Sm−1S^{m-1} such that

(𝒫¯∖𝒪)∩Toricα⁡(N)¯=∅,({\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\setminus\mathcal{O})\cap{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(N)}}=\emptyset,

where the two closures are taken in the compactification [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m}.

Proof.

For positive integers nn, let {Nn}\left\{N_{n}\right\} denote a shrinking sequence of εn\varepsilon_{n}-neighborhoods of H⟂∩Sm−1H^{\perp}\cap S^{m-1} in Sm−1S^{m-1} with radius εn>0\varepsilon_{n}>0 tending to 0. (For instance, take εn=1/n\varepsilon_{n}=1/n.) It suffices to show that the set

𝒬n=(𝒫¯∖𝒪)∩Toricα⁡(Nn)¯\mathcal{Q}_{n}=({\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\setminus\mathcal{O})\cap{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(N_{n})}}

is empty for some nn. The intersection of the sets 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} for all nn is (𝒫¯∖𝒪)∩Toricα⁡(H)¯({\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\setminus\mathcal{O})\cap{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(H)}}, which is empty by Theorem 5.16. Since the sets 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} are nested closed subsets of the compact space [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m}, a standard theorem of topology (see Theorem 26.9 and the ensuing discussion in the book by Munkres [36]) implies that 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} is empty for large nn. ∎

Theorem 5.17 implies that if a toric ray Toricα⁡(w)\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(w) intersects 𝒫\mathcal{P} outside of a neighborhood of the Birch point qq, then ww lies outside a neighborhood of H⟂H^{\perp}, so the H⟂H^{\perp}-component of ww is not too dominant. We quantify this via a lower bound on the HH-component. For notation, every vector w∈ℝmw\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is uniquely expressible as the sum wH+wH⟂w_{H}+w_{H^{\perp}} of a vector wH∈Hw_{H}\in H and a vector wH⟂∈H⟂w_{H^{\perp}}\in H^{\perp}.

Corollary 5.18.

Fix a linear subspace H⊆ℝmH\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and α,p∈ℝ>0m\alpha,p\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}. For every open subset 𝒪\mathcal{O} of the interior of the polyhedron 𝒫=(p+H)∩ℝ≥0m\mathcal{P}=(p+H)\cap\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0} such that 𝒪\mathcal{O} contains the α\alpha-Birch point, there exists μ>0\mu>0 such that ∥wH∥≥μ\lVert w_{H}\rVert\geq\mu for all unit vectors ww satisfying α∗θw∈int⁡(𝒫)∖𝒪\alpha*\theta^{w}\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\setminus\mathcal{O} for some θ>1\theta>1.

Proof.

By the proof of Theorem 5.17, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that the ε\varepsilon-neighborhood NN of H⟂∩Sm−1H^{\perp}\cap S^{m-1} in Sm−1S^{m-1} satisfies (𝒫¯∖𝒪)∩Toricα⁡(N)¯=∅({\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\setminus\mathcal{O})\cap{\overline{\operatorname{Toric}_{\alpha}(N)}}=\emptyset. Now define

μ=inf{∥wH∥|w∈Sm−1∖N}.\mu=\inf\big\{\lVert w_{H}\rVert\,\big|\,w\in S^{m-1}\setminus N\big\}.

Then μ>0\mu>0 because it is the infimum of a nonnegative continuous function on a compact set that never takes the value 00 because wH=0⇒w∈H⟂⊆Nw_{H}=0\Rightarrow w\in H^{\perp}\subseteq N. If α∗θw∈int⁡(𝒫)∖𝒪\alpha*\theta^{w}\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\setminus\mathcal{O}, then w∉Nw\notin N by construction of NN, so ∥wH∥≥μ\lVert w_{H}\rVert\geq\mu by definition of μ\mu. ∎

Remark 5.19.

Corollary 5.18 can be extended so that it also considers the case when the closure in [0,∞]m[0,\infty]^{m} of a toric ray intersects 𝒫¯∖𝒪{\overline{\mathcal{P}}}\setminus\mathcal{O}. However, we do not need this extension in the following section.

Remark 5.20.

Müller and Regensburger gave an extension of Birch’s theorem [35, Proposition 3.9] that is different from those presented here (Theorems 5.16 and 5.17). Their result was used to generalize results about complex-balanced systems to the setting of certain generalized mass-action ODE systems.

6 Jets

This section introduces the technology of jets to relate the combinatorial geometry of reaction diagrams to the dynamics. Using this connection, we prove that for strongly endotactic reaction networks, the “draining” reactions—those that pose a threat to persistence—are dominated by “sustaining” reactions (Proposition 6.26).

6.1 Jet frames, unit jets, and toric jets

Recall the meaning of θw=θw1⋯θwn\theta^{w}=\theta^{w_{1}}\cdots\theta^{w_{n}} from Notation 5.1, where w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and θ∈ℝ>0\theta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. Recall also the geometric interpretation, from Remarks 5.4 and 5.5, of ww and log⁡θ\log\theta together comprising polar coordinates on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

The following notations are standard.

Notation 6.1.

The phrase “for large ii” is shorthand for “for all ii greater than some fixed constant i0i_{0}”. For two sequences (f⁡(i))(f(i)) and (g⁡(i))(g(i)) taking values in ℝ\mathbb{R},

  1. 1.

    f⁡(i)=O⁡(g⁡(i))f(i)=O(g(i)) if there exists c>0c>0 such that |f⁡(i)|≤c​|g⁡(i)||f(i)|\leq c|g(i)| for large ii,

  2. 2.

    f⁡(i)=Ω⁡(g⁡(i))f(i)=\Omega(g(i)) if there exists c>0c>0 such that |f⁡(i)|≥c​|g⁡(i)||f(i)|\geq c|g(i)| for large ii, and

  3. 3.

    f⁡(i)=Θ⁡(g⁡(i))f(i)=\Theta(g(i)) if there exist c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that c1​|g⁡(i)|≤|f⁡(i)|≤c2​|g⁡(i)|c_{1}|g(i)|\leq|f(i)|\leq c_{2}|g(i)| for large ii.

Following standard practice, we allow the above notations to appear in expressions and inequalities. For instance, f⁡(i)≥g⁡(i)+O⁡(h⁡(i))f(i)\geq g(i)+O(h(i)) means that f⁡(i)≥g⁡(i)+k⁡(i)f(i)\geq g(i)+k(i) for some k⁡(i)=O⁡(h⁡(i))k(i)=O(h(i)).

Our next definition introduces jets and toric jets. We first fix an orthonormal basis, a frame. Intuitively, a jet consists of a sequence of points that, to first order, are pointing in the direction of the first basis vector, with a small perturbation in the second direction, with an even smaller perturbation in the third direction, and so on. A toric jet is obtained by coordinate-wise exponentiation of a jet.

Toric jets serve as test sequences that allow us to deduce persistence. To prove that a certain function is Lyapunov-like, it is not enough to analyze the function along one direction; perturbations around that direction require exploration, as well. It turns out that the perturbations allowed in toric jets are general enough, while at the same time the gradient of the function x​log⁡x−xx\log x-x along a toric jet is easy to analyze; see the proof of Theorem 7.5.

Definition 6.2.

Let n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.

  1. 1.

    A frame is a list w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) of mutually orthogonal unit vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  2. 2.

    A jet is a sequence (w⁡(i))i∈ℤ>0(w(i))_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}} of vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} in the positive span of some frame w¯{\overline{w}} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (i.e., ⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩>0\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle>0 for all ii and jj) such that for j=1,…,ℓ−1j=1,\ldots,\ell-1, the limit limi→∞⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩⟨w⁡(i),wj+1⟩\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\frac{\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle}{\langle w(i),w_{j+1}\rangle} exists and equals +∞+\infty. A unit jet is a jet that consists of unit vectors.

  3. 3.

    A toric jet is a sequence (θ​(i)w⁡(i))i∈ℤ>0\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}, where (w⁡(i))(w(i)) is a unit jet in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and (θ⁡(i))(\theta(i)) is a sequence in ℝ>1\mathbb{R}_{>1} with limi→∞θ⁡(i)=+∞\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\theta(i)=+\infty.

The jet frame for the jet (w⁡(i))(w(i)) or toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) is w¯{\overline{w}}, and these jets are framed by w¯{\overline{w}}.

Remark 6.3.

Toric jets have a geometric interpretation: the sequence

(log⁡θ⁡(i))​w​(i)=(log⁡θ⁡(i))​(β1​(n)​w1+⋯+βℓ​(n)​wℓ)\displaystyle\big(\log\theta(i)\big)w(i)=(\log\theta(i))\big(\beta_{1}({n})w_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{\ell}({n})w_{\ell}\big) (11)

is to first approximation a sequence going to infinity in direction w1w_{1} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, which is viewed as “energy space”; the second-order correction is in direction w2w_{2}, and so on. Exponentiating the sequence (11) yields the toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) in “concentration space” ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}.

In the context of a reaction network, if the image of a toric jet lies in a given invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}, then the toric jet necessarily approaches the boundary of 𝒫\mathcal{P} or is unbounded. More precisely, (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) approaches the boundary of the closure 𝒫¯{\overline{\mathcal{P}}} of 𝒫\mathcal{P} in the compactification [0,∞]𝒮[0,\infty]^{\mathcal{S}}. Our approach to proving persistence is to demonstrate that no toric jet is a sequence of points along a trajectory (see the proof of Theorem 7.5). This strategy is a distillation of the argument employed by Anderson in [4].

Remark 6.4.

The concepts of jet frame and unit jet were introduced by Miller and Pak in [34, Definition 4.1] for the purpose of describing the interaction of an expanding wavefront on the boundary of a convex polytope infinitesimally after the wavefront hits a new face. Our definitions are related but not identical to theirs.

Example 6.5.

Every sequence of points θ​(i)w\theta(i)^{w} along a toric ray with θ⁡(i)→∞\theta(i)\to\infty is a special case of a toric jet. Here the jet frame is the singleton list containing only the direction ww of the toric ray.

We now give two lemmas concerning unit jets.

Lemma 6.6.

If (w⁡(i))(w(i)) is a unit jet with frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}), then w⁡(i)→w1w(i)\to w_{1} as i→∞i\to\infty.

Proof.

Let w⁡(i)=∑j=1ℓβj​(i)​wjw(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}, where βj​(i)>0\beta_{j}({i})>0. By definition, βj​(i)βj+1​(i)→∞\frac{\beta_{j}(i)}{\beta_{j+1}(i)}\to\infty for j=1,…,ℓ−1j=1,\ldots,\ell-1. As every w⁡(i)w(i) and wjw_{j} is a unit vector, it follows that β1​(i)→1\beta_{1}(i)\to 1, and all other βj​(i)→0\beta_{j}(i)\to 0 (for j=2,…,ℓj=2,\ldots,\ell). ∎

Lemma 6.7 (Unit jets are abundant).

Let n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Every infinite sequence of unit vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has an infinite subsequence that is a unit jet.

Proof.

Let (w⁡(i))(w(i)) be an infinite sequence of unit vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Throughout this proof, subsequences of (w⁡(i))(w(i)) are denoted again by (w⁡(i))(w(i)) for ease of notation. We proceed by induction on nn.

For n=1n=1, if the sequence (w⁡(i))(w(i)) takes the value +1+1 infinitely often, then choose w1w_{1} to be +1+1. Otherwise w⁡(i)w(i) takes the value −1-1 infinitely often, so choose w1w_{1} to be −1-1. The required unit jet is the constant subsequence (w⁡(i)=w1)(w(i)=w_{1}) with frame w¯=(w1){\overline{w}}=(w_{1}).

Now assume that n≥2n\geq 2. As the sequence w⁡(i)w(i) lies in the unit sphere, which is compact, the sequence must have an accumulation point, which we denote by w1w_{1}. Restricting to a subsequence if necessary, assume that limi→∞w⁡(i)=w1\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}w(i)=w_{1}.

Let β1​(i)=⟨w⁡(i),w1⟩\beta_{1}({i})=\langle w(i),w_{1}\rangle. Then limi→∞β1​(i)=⟨w1,w1⟩=1\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\beta_{1}({i})=\langle w_{1},w_{1}\rangle=1. Take a subsequence with β1​(i)>0\beta_{1}({i})>0 for all ii. Consider the sequence (w′​(i)=w⁡(i)−β1​(i)​w1)(w^{\prime}(i)=w(i)-\beta_{1}({i})w_{1}).

Case 1. For large ii, the sequence (w′​(i))(w^{\prime}(i)) is the zero vector. Then for large ii, w⁡(i)=β1​(i)​w1w(i)=\beta_{1}({i})w_{1}, so this subsequence is a unit jet with frame w¯=(w1){\overline{w}}=(w_{1}).

Case 2. The sequence (w′​(i))(w^{\prime}(i)) is nonzero infinitely often. Then restrict to a subsequence that is always nonzero. By induction, the sequence of unit vectors w′​(i)/‖w′​(i)‖w^{\prime}(i)/||w^{\prime}(i)|| in w1⟂≅ℝn−1w_{1}^{\perp}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n-1} has a subsequence with frame (w2,…,wℓ)⊆w1⟂(w_{2},\ldots,w_{\ell})\subseteq w_{1}^{\perp} and corresponding positive coefficients β~j​(i)\widetilde{\beta}_{j}(i) for j=2,…,ℓj=2,\ldots,\ell such that w′​(i)/‖w′​(i)‖=∑j=2ℓβ~j​(i)​wjw^{\prime}(i)/||w^{\prime}(i)||=\sum_{j=2}^{\ell}\widetilde{\beta}_{j}(i)w_{j} is a unit jet.

For j=2,…,ℓj=2,\ldots,\ell, let βj​(i)=β~j​(i)⋅‖w′​(i)‖\beta_{j}({i})=\widetilde{\beta}_{j}(i)\cdot||w^{\prime}(i)||. We claim that the corresponding subsequence defined by w⁡(i)=β1​(i)​w1+∑j=2ℓβj​(i)​wjw(i)=\beta_{1}({i})w_{1}+\sum_{j=2}^{\ell}\beta_{j}({i})w_{j} is a unit jet framed by (w1,…,wℓ)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}). We need only check that the first coefficient dominates the second. To see that it does, note that β2​(i)=β~2​(i)⋅∥w′​(i)∥\beta_{2}({i})=\widetilde{\beta}_{2}(i)\cdot\lVert w^{\prime}(i)\rVert converges to 00, because β~2​(i)→1\widetilde{\beta}_{2}(i)\to 1 by definition of jet frame and ‖w′​(i)‖→0||w^{\prime}(i)||\to 0 by definition of w1w_{1} and β1\beta_{1}. Hence β1​(i)/β2​(i)→∞\beta_{1}({i})/\beta_{2}({i})\to\infty because β1​(i)→1\beta_{1}({i})\to 1. ∎

6.2 Geometry of jets

Theorem 6.11 in this subsection conveys an important geometric idea behind jets. Later we use this result to prove a useful characterization of endotactic networks (Lemma 6.22). We begin with some preliminaries.

Definition 6.8.

Fix a positive integer n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, a finite set Q⊆ℝnQ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, and a list w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) of vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Set Super0⁡(Q,w¯)=Q\operatorname{Super}_{0}(Q,{\overline{w}})=Q, and inductively for j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell let Superj⁡(Q,w¯)\operatorname{Super}_{j}(Q,{\overline{w}}) denote the set of ≤wj\leq_{w_{j}}-maximal elements of Superj−1⁡(Q,w¯)\operatorname{Super}_{j-1}(Q,{\overline{w}}).

Notation 6.9.

When the set QQ and the list w¯{\overline{w}} of vectors is clear from context, we write Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j} to denote Superj⁡(Q,w¯)\operatorname{Super}_{j}(Q,{\overline{w}}).

Lemma 6.10.

Fix a positive integer n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, a frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, a unit jet (w⁡(i)=∑j=1ℓβj​(i)​wj)(w(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}) framed by w¯{\overline{w}}, and a finite set Q⊆ℝnQ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}. Let λ∈{1,…,ℓ}\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}.

  1. 1.

    If x∈Superλx\in\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda} and y∉Superλy\notin\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda}, then there exists k∈{1,…,λ}k\in\{1,\ldots,\lambda\} such that ⟨wk,x−y⟩>0\langle w_{k},x-y\rangle>0 and ⟨wj,x−y⟩=0\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle=0 for all j=1,…,k−1j=1,\ldots,k-1. Consequently, ⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩>0\langle w(i),x-y\rangle>0 for large ii, and ⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩=Ω⁡(βk​(i))\langle w(i),x-y\rangle=\Omega(\beta_{k}(i)).

  2. 2.

    If λ>1\lambda>1 and x∈Superλ−1x\in\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda-1} and y∈Qy\in Q, then for large ii,

    ⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩≥∑j=λℓβj​(i)​⟨wj,x−y⟩.\displaystyle\langle w(i),x-y\rangle\geq\sum_{j=\lambda}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle. (12)
Proof.

1. Suppose x∈Superλx\in\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda} and y∉Superλy\notin\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda}. Let k∈{1,…,λ}k\in\{1,\ldots,\lambda\} be the smallest positive integer such that y∉Superky\notin\operatorname{Super}_{k}. It follows that ⟨wk,x−y⟩>0\langle w_{k},x-y\rangle>0 because y∈Superk−1∖Superky\in\operatorname{Super}_{k-1}\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{k} and x∈Superkx\in\operatorname{Super}_{k}. Further, ⟨wj,x−y⟩=0\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle=0 for all j<kj<k, since x,y∈Superjx,y\in\operatorname{Super}_{j} for j<kj<k. Thus

⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩=∑j=1ℓβj​(i)​⟨wj,x−y⟩=βk​(i)​⟨wk,x−y⟩+O⁡(βk+1​(i)),\langle w(i),x-y\rangle\ =\ \sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle\ =\ \beta_{k}(i)\langle w_{k},x-y\rangle+O(\beta_{k+1}(i)),

where βℓ+1​(i)\beta_{\ell+1}(i) is understood to be 00. Thus, ⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩>0\langle w(i),x-y\rangle>0 for large ii because ⟨wk,x−y⟩>0\langle w_{k},x-y\rangle>0 and, by definition of unit jet, βk​(i)>0\beta_{k}(i)>0 and βk+1​(i)/βk​(i)→0\beta_{k+1}(i)/\beta_{k}(i)\to 0 as i→∞i\to\infty. Additionally, it follows that ⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩=Ω⁡(βk​(i))\langle w(i),x-y\rangle=\Omega(\beta_{k}(i)).

2. Suppose x∈Superλ−1x\in\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda-1}. Set

ϕ⁡(i)=∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​⟨wj,x−y⟩,\phi(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle,

and rewrite inequality (12) as ϕ⁡(i)≥0\phi(i)\geq 0. If y∈Superλ−1y\in\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda-1}, then ⟨wj,x−y⟩=0\langle w_{j},x-y\rangle=0 for j=1,…,λ−1j=1,\ldots,\lambda-1, so in fact ϕ⁡(i)=0\phi(i)=0. If y∉Superλ−1y\notin\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda-1}, then consider the sequence defined by

v⁡(i)=∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​wj‖∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​wj‖,v(i)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}}{||\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}||},

which is a unit jet framed by (w1,…,wλ−1)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\lambda-1}) by construction, using the fact that (w⁡(i))(w(i)) is a unit jet. Then

ϕ⁡(i)=‖∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​wj‖​⟨v⁡(i),x−y⟩.\displaystyle\phi(i)=\Big\|\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}\Big\|\langle v(i),x-y\rangle. (13)

Of the terms in (13), ∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​wj\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j} approaches w1w_{1} (by definition of unit jet), so its norm ‖∑j=1λ−1βj​(i)​wj‖||\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda-1}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}|| approaches 11, and ⟨v⁡(i),x−y⟩>0\langle v(i),x-y\rangle>0 for large ii by part 1 of this lemma. So ϕ⁡(i)>0\phi(i)>0 for large ii, and inequality (12) holds. ∎

The next result and Corollary 6.12 may be seen as generalizations of Proposition 2.3(iii) in Ziegler’s Lectures on Polytopes [51]; with more careful accounting, we obtain our required stronger result. An alternative, direct proof of Corollary 6.12 follows the same lines as the proof in Ziegler’s book, without appealing to jets.

Theorem 6.11 (Fundamental theorem of jets).

Fix a positive integer n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, a frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, a unit jet (v⁡(i)=∑j=1ℓβj​(i)​wj)\big(v(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}\big) framed by w¯{\overline{w}}, and a finite set Q⊆ℝnQ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then for large ii, the ≤v⁡(i)\leq_{v(i)}-maximal subset of QQ equals Superℓ\operatorname{Super}_{\ell}.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on ℓ\ell. More precisely, for j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell, let (vj​(i))(v_{j}(i)) be the jet

vj​(i)=β1​(i)​w1+⋯+βj​(i)​wj.v_{j}(i)=\beta_{1}(i)w_{1}+\dots+\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}.

We prove that for all j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell, the ≤vj​(i)\leq_{v_{j}(i)}-maximal subset of QQ equals Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j} for large ii. The base case of the induction—that Super1\operatorname{Super}_{1} is the ≤v1​(i)\leq_{v_{1}(i)}-maximal subset of QQ for large ii—is true by definition of Super1\operatorname{Super}_{1} because v1​(i)→w1v_{1}(i)\to w_{1}.

Fix j<ℓj<\ell and assume that the ≤vj​(i)\leq_{v_{j}(i)}-maximal subset of QQ equals Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j} for large ii. From now on, consider only such sufficiently large ii. For x∈Superjx\in\operatorname{Super}_{j}, let c⁡(i)=⟨vj​(i),x⟩c{}(i)=\langle v_{j}(i),x\rangle be the value of the inner product of vj​(i)v_{j}(i) with every element in Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j}; informally, write c⁡(i)=⟨vj​(i),Superj⟩c{}(i)=\langle v_{j}(i),\operatorname{Super}_{j}\rangle. Similarly, let c′∈ℝc^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} denote the value of the inner product of wj+1w_{j+1} with every element in Superj+1\operatorname{Super}_{j+1}; informally, write c′=⟨wj+1,Superj+1⟩c^{\prime}=\langle w_{j+1},\operatorname{Super}_{j+1}\rangle. Next, define δ⁡(i)\delta(i) to be the reciprocal of left-hand side of the inequality

1δ⁡(i)=maxy∈Q∖Superj⁡max⁡{0,⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′}c⁡(i)−⟨vj​(i),y⟩≤maxy∈Q∖Superj⁡{0,⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′}miny∈Q∖Superj⁡(c⁡(i)−⟨vj​(i),y⟩).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\delta(i)}=\max_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}\frac{\max\{0,\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\}}{c{}(i)-\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle}\leq\frac{\max_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}\{0,\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\}}{\min_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}(c{}(i)-\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle)}. (14)

If 1/δ⁡(i)=01/\delta(i)=0, then declare δ⁡(i)=+∞\delta(i)=+\infty. Note that δ⁡(i)>0\delta(i)>0 for large ii, because the denominators in (14) are strictly positive by the inductive hypothesis, and the numerators are nonnegative by construction. The numerator on the right-hand side of (14) has no dependence on ii, and hence is O⁡(1)O(1). Also, using the identity ⟨vj​(i),x⟩=c⁡(i)\langle v_{j}(i),x\rangle=c{}(i) for x∈Superjx\in\operatorname{Super}_{j}, the denominator on the right-hand side of (14) satisfies

miny∈Q∖Superj⁡(c⁡(i)−⟨vj​(i),y⟩)=miny∈Q∖Superjx∈Superj⁡⟨vj​(i),x−y⟩=Ω⁡(βj​(i)),\displaystyle\min_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}\big(c{}(i)-\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle\big)=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}\\ x\in\operatorname{Super}_{j}\\[-0.75346pt] \end{subarray}}\langle v_{j}(i),x-y\rangle=\Omega\big(\beta_{j}(i)\big),

where the second equality follows from Lemma 6.10.1. Thus the inequality (14) yields

δ⁡(i)≥miny∈Q∖Superj⁡(c⁡(i)−⟨vj​(i),y⟩)maxy∈Q∖Superj⁡{0,⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′}=Ω​(βj​(i))O⁡(1)=Ω⁡(βj​(i)).\delta(i)\geq\frac{\min_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}\big(c{}(i)-\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle\big)}{\max_{y\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}}\{0,\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\}}=\frac{\Omega\big(\beta_{j}(i)\big)}{O(1)}=\Omega\big(\beta_{j}(i)\big).

Hence, by the definition of jet, δ​(i)>βj+1​(i)\delta(i)>\beta_{j+1}(i) for large ii.

We now complete the proof by proving that for large ii, the following inequality holds for all y∈Qy\in Q and achieves equality exactly on the set Superj+1\operatorname{Super}_{j+1}:

⟨vj+1​(i),y⟩=⟨vj​(i),y⟩+βj+1​(i)​⟨wj+1,y⟩≤c⁡(i)+βj+1​(i)​c′.\displaystyle\langle v_{j+1}(i),y\rangle=\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle+\beta_{j+1}(i)\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle\leq c{}(i)+\beta_{j+1}(i)c^{\prime}. (15)

If y∈Superjy\in\operatorname{Super}_{j}, then ⟨vj​(i),y⟩=c⁡(i)\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle=c{}(i) by definition and ⟨wj+1,y⟩≤c′\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle\leq c^{\prime} by construction, with equality holding precisely when y∈Superj+1y\in\operatorname{Super}_{j+1}; hence the desired (in)equality in (15) holds. Now assume that y∈Q∖Superjy\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j}. There are two subcases based on the sign of ⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}. First, if ⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′<0\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}<0, then the inequality in (15) is strict, noting that ⟨vj​(i),y⟩≤c⁡(i)\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle\leq c{}(i) because y∈Qy\in Q. In the remaining case, when y∈Q∖Superjy\in Q\setminus\operatorname{Super}_{j} and ⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′≥0\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\geq 0, the construction of δ⁡(i)\delta(i) in (14) yields the first of the inequalities

c⁡(i)−⟨vj​(i),y⟩≥δ⁡(i)​(⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′)>βj+1​(i)​(⟨wj+1,y⟩−c′),\displaystyle c{}(i)-\langle v_{j}(i),y\rangle\geq\delta(i)\big(\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\big)>\beta_{j+1}(i)\big(\langle w_{j+1},y\rangle-c^{\prime}\big), (16)

while the second inequality is due to the inequality δ​(i)>βj+1​(i)\delta(i)>\beta_{j+1}(i) proven earlier. Rearranging (16) yields the desired strict inequality in (15). ∎

Corollary 6.12.

Fix a positive integer n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, a frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and a finite set Q⊆ℝnQ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}. There exist β1,…,βℓ∈ℝ>0\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and a positive linear combination w~=β1​w1+⋯+βℓ​wℓ\widetilde{w}=\beta_{1}w_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{\ell}w_{\ell} such that the set of ≤w~\leq_{\widetilde{w}}-maximal elements of QQ equals Superℓ\operatorname{Super}_{\ell}. Additionally, if γ1,…,γℓ∈ℝ>0\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, then β1,…,βℓ\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{\ell} can be chosen so that βj<γj​βj−1\beta_{j}<\gamma_{j}\beta_{j-1} for all j=2,…,ℓj=2,\dots,\ell.

Proof.

Use Theorem 6.11: first consider a jet (w⁡(i))(w(i)) in the frame w¯{\overline{w}}, and then define w~\widetilde{w} as w⁡(i0)w(i_{0}) for a sufficiently large value of i0i_{0}, and use the definition of jet. ∎

Remark 6.13.

The hypotheses of Corollary 6.12 can be weakened. The corollary remains true for any set QQ whose convex hull is a polytope and for any list of vectors (w1,…,wℓ)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) that need not be orthonormal. Indeed, this is the setting of the analogous result in Ziegler’s book [51, Proposition 2.3(iii)]. We do not need this generality here.

Example 6.14.

We illustrate Corollary 6.12 by considering the set QQ consisting of the six vertices of a hexagon:

The set Q1Q_{1} consists of the two vertices on the edge that is the ≤w1\leq_{w_{1}}-maximal face of the hexagon, and the vertex Q2Q_{2} is the ≤w2\leq_{w_{2}}-maximal subset of Q1Q_{1}. For 0<ε<δ=30<\varepsilon<\delta=\sqrt{3}, the vertex Q2Q_{2} is the ≤w1+ε​w2\leq_{w_{1}+\varepsilon w_{2}}-maximal subset of QQ. In other words, w1+ε​w2w_{1}+\varepsilon w_{2} defines Q2Q_{2} as long as it lies between w1w_{1} and the dotted arrow depicted twice in the figure above.

6.3 Jets and reactions

One of our primary goals, carried out in Section 7, is to prove that given a strongly endotactic network, there is a compact set outside of which the function g⁡(x)=∑i∈𝒮xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} decreases along trajectories; that is, its derivative along trajectories is negative (Theorem 7.5). Intuitively, this derivative is a sum of contributions (“pulls”; Definition 6.18) from each reaction (see the proof of Lemma 7.4). A “draining” reaction acts to hinder our efforts (Definition 6.15) with a positive pull. The pull of a “sustaining” reaction is negative. Proposition 6.26 shows that, after fixing a toric jet, each draining reaction is dominated by some sustaining reaction, so negativity prevails overall and g⁡(x)g(x) indeed decreases.

Definition 6.15.

For a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), let w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) be a frame in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}.

  1. 1.

    A reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} is w¯{\overline{w}}-essential if ⟨wj,y′−y⟩≠0\langle w_{j},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\neq 0 for some j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell.

  2. 2.

    The level of a w¯{\overline{w}}-essential reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is the least jj such that ⟨wj,y′−y⟩≠0\langle w_{j},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\neq 0.

  3. 3.

    A w¯{\overline{w}}-essential reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} with level λ\lambda is

    1. (a)

      w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining if ⟨wλ,y′−y⟩<0\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0.

    2. (b)

      w¯{\overline{w}}-draining if ⟨wλ,y′−y⟩>0\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle>0.

Remark 6.16.

For a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) and a nonzero vector ww in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}, a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} is (w)(w)-essential (Definition 6.15.1) if and only if y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is ww-essential (Definition 3.9.3). More generally, for a frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}, a reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-essential if and only if y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is wjw_{j}-essential for some j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell.

Example 6.17.

For network GG of Figure 2 in Section 3, let w¯=(w1,w2){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},w_{2}) be a frame with w1=ww_{1}=w, where ww is depicted in Figure 2. Then reaction y2→y2′y_{2}\to y_{2}^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-draining, and y3→y3′y_{3}\to y_{3}^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining. Whether y1→y1′y_{1}\to y_{1}^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining or w¯{\overline{w}}-draining depends on whether ⟨w2,y1′−y1⟩\langle w_{2},y_{1}^{\prime}-y_{1}\rangle is negative or positive.

Definition 6.18.

Let G=(𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)G=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a reaction network.

  1. 1.

    The pull of a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} along a toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} is the function

    pully→y′⁡(i)=⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩​θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),y⟩.\displaystyle\operatorname{pull}\limits_{y\to y^{\prime}}(i)=\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),y\rangle}. (17)
  2. 2.

    A unit jet (w⁡(i))(w(i)) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} is adapted to GG if for every reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}, either

    1. (a)

      ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩=0\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for all ii; or

    2. (b)

      ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩<0\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0 for all ii, in which case y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is sustaining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)); or

    3. (c)

      ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩>0\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle>0 for all ii, in which case y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is draining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)).

    A reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is essential along (w⁡(i))(w(i)) if it is sustaining or draining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)).

  3. 3.

    A toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) framed by (w1,…,wℓ)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} is adapted to GG if its unit jet (w⁡(i))(w(i)) is adapted to GG and, for all j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell, the limit limi→∞θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle} exists in [1,∞][1,\infty].

  4. 4.

    A reaction r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} dominates a reaction r′∈ℛr^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} along a toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} if the ratio of their pulls along (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) tends to infinity in absolute value: limi→∞|pullr⁡(i)pullr′⁡(i)|\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\Big|\frac{\operatorname{pull}\limits_{r}(i)}{\operatorname{pull}\limits_{r^{\prime}}(i)}\Big| exists and equals +∞+\infty.

When the toric jet is clear from context, we simply say that reaction rr dominates reaction r′r^{\prime}.

Lemma 6.19.

Fix a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}). Let w⁡(i)w(i) be a unit jet in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and let (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) be a toric jet in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}.

  1. 1.

    There exists an infinite subsequence of w⁡(i)w(i) that is adapted to (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}).

  2. 2.

    There exists an infinite subsequence of (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) that is adapted to (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}).

Proof.

Repeatedly take subsequences, first so that for each reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}, the sign of ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle is constant for all ii, and then so that for all j=1,…,ℓj=1,\ldots,\ell, an accumulation point of θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle} becomes a limit point. We can do this because θ⁡(i)>1\theta(i)>1 and ⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩>0\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle>0 for all ii, whence θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),wj⟩\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),w_{j}\rangle} lies in the compact set [1,∞][1,\infty]. ∎

It is equivalent for a reaction to be essential along a unit jet or with respect to its jet frame, if the unit jet is adapted to the relevant network. Here is a more precise statement.

Proposition 6.20.

Let G=(𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)G=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a reaction network, and let (w⁡(i))(w(i)) be a unit jet adapted to GG and framed by w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}). Let λ∈{1,…,ℓ}\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}.

  1. 1.

    A reaction is w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining (respectively, w¯{\overline{w}}-draining) if and only if it is sustaining (respectively, draining) along (w⁡(i))(w(i)).

  2. 2.

    A w¯{\overline{w}}-essential reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} has level λ\lambda if and only if |⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩|=Θ⁡(⟨w⁡(i),wλ⟩)|\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle|=\Theta\big(\langle w(i),w_{\lambda}\rangle\big).

Proof.

Let w⁡(i)=∑j=1ℓβj​(i)​wjw(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\beta_{j}(i)w_{j}. Consider a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}.

If y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is not w¯{\overline{w}}-essential then ⟨wj,y′−y⟩=0\langle w_{j},y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for all jj, and in that case ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩=0\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for all ii, so y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is not essential along (w⁡(i))(w(i)).

Next assume y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-essential with level λ\lambda, so ⟨wλ,y′−y⟩=0\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for all j<λj<\lambda whereas ⟨wλ,y′−y⟩≠0\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\neq 0, where the inequality is “<<” in the sustaining case and “>>” in the draining case. Thus ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩=βλ​(i)​⟨wλ,y′−y⟩+O⁡(βλ+1​(i))\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle=\beta_{\lambda}(i)\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle+O(\beta_{\lambda+1}(i)), so ⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle is nonzero for large ii by the definition of unit jet—again, with <0<0 in the sustaining case and >0>0 in the draining case. Hence y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is essential along (w⁡(i))(w(i)) if it is w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining and draining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)) if it is w¯{\overline{w}}-draining, and in either case |⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩|=Θ⁡(βλ​(i))=Θ⁡(⟨w⁡(i),wλ⟩)|\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle|=\Theta(\beta_{\lambda}(i))=\Theta(\langle w(i),w_{\lambda}\rangle). That takes care of the “⇒\Rightarrow” direction of part 2.

For the “⇐\Leftarrow” direction of part 2, suppose that the reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-essential and that |⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩|=Θ⁡(βλ​(i))|\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle|=\Theta(\beta_{\lambda}(i)). It follows that ⟨wj,y′−y⟩=0\langle w_{j},y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for all j<λj<\lambda, and ⟨wλ,y′−y⟩≠0\langle w_{\lambda},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\neq 0, so y→y′y\to y^{\prime} has level λ\lambda. ∎

6.4 Jets and endotactic networks

The next two results interpret endotactic and strongly endotactic networks in terms of jets.

Notation 6.21.

For a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) and jet frame w¯={w1,…,wℓ}{\overline{w}}=\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}\}, denote by Super1\operatorname{Super}_{1} the ≤w1\leq_{w_{1}}-maximal subset of reactant⁡(ℛ)\operatorname{reactant}(\mathcal{R}), and for j∈{2,…,ℓ}j\in\{2,\ldots,\ell\}, write Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j} for the ≤wj\leq_{w_{j}}-maximal subset of Superj−1\operatorname{Super}_{j-1}.

In other words, the sets Superj\operatorname{Super}_{j} coincide with those in Section 6.2, where Q=reactant⁡(ℛ)Q=\operatorname{reactant}(\mathcal{R}).

Lemma 6.22.

Let (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a reaction network.

  1. 1.

    (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is endotactic if and only if for every singleton frame (w1)(w_{1}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and for every (w1)(w_{1})-draining reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} in ℛ\mathcal{R}, there exists a (w1)(w_{1})-sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} such that ⟨w1,x−y⟩>0\langle w_{1},x-y\rangle>0.

  2. 2.

    If (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is endotactic, then for every frame w¯{\overline{w}} in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and every w¯{\overline{w}}-draining reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} in ℛ\mathcal{R} with level λ\lambda, the reactant yy lies outside of Superλ\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda}.

Proof.

1. The network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) fails to be endotactic if and only if there is a unit vector w1w_{1} in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with y∈suppw1⁡(𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)y\in\operatorname{supp}_{w_{1}}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) such that ⟨w1,y′−y⟩>0\langle w_{1},y^{\prime}-y\rangle>0 (recall Definition 3.14). Equivalently, (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) fails to be endotactic precisely when there is a unit vector w1w_{1} in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and a (w1)(w_{1})-draining reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} such that every (w1)(w_{1})-sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} satisfies y≤wxy\leq_{w}x. Now use that y≤wx⇔⟨w1,x−y⟩≤0y\leq_{w}x\Leftrightarrow\langle w_{1},x-y\rangle\leq 0.

2. Suppose (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is endotactic. Consider a frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}. Suppose y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-draining and has level λ\lambda. By Corollary 6.12, Superλ\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda} is the ≤w∗\leq_{w^{*}}-maximal subset of Super0=reactant⁡(ℛ)\operatorname{Super}_{0}=\operatorname{reactant}(\mathcal{R}), where w∗=w1+ε1​w2+⋯+ελ−1​wλw^{*}=w_{1}+\varepsilon_{1}w_{2}+\cdots+\varepsilon_{\lambda-1}w_{\lambda} for some positive numbers ε1,…,ελ−1\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{\lambda-1}. Corollary 6.12 allows us to choose all of ε1,…,ελ−1\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{\lambda-1} to be arbitrarily small, so we can ensure that ⟨w∗,y′−y⟩\langle w^{*},y^{\prime}-y\rangle has the same sign as ⟨w1,y′−y⟩\langle w_{1},y^{\prime}-y\rangle, which is positive. Then, from the definition of w∗w^{*}-endotactic, we conclude that y∉Superλy\notin\operatorname{Super}_{\lambda}. ∎

Example 6.23.

The converse of Lemma 6.22.2 is false. For the 1-dimensional network

the essential reactions (if any) corresponding to both (singleton) frames (w)(w) and (−w)(-w) are sustaining. Proposition 6.24.

For an endotactic reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) with stoichiometric subspace HH, the following are equivalent.

  1. 1.

    (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is strongly endotactic.

  2. 2.

    For every singleton jet frame (w1)(w_{1}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} with w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}, there exists a (w1)(w_{1})-sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} such that x∈Super1x\in\operatorname{Super}_{1}.

  3. 3.

    For every frame w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} with w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}, there exists a w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} with x∈Superℓx\in\operatorname{Super}_{\ell}.

Proof.

The equivalence of items 1 and 2 is straightforward from the definition of strongly endotactic, and item 2 is a special case of item 3. We therefore assume item 1, with the goal of deducing item 3. Let w¯=(w1,…,wℓ){\overline{w}}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) be a frame in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} with w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}. Let (w⁡(i))(w(i)) be a unit jet framed by w¯{\overline{w}}. Use Lemma 6.19.1 to pick a subsequence of (w⁡(i))(w(i)) adapted to (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}). Using the fundamental theorem of jets (Theorem 6.11), take i0i_{0} large enough so that the ≤w⁡(i0)\leq_{w(i_{0})}-maximal subset of reactant⁡(ℛ)\operatorname{reactant}(\mathcal{R}) equals Superℓ\operatorname{Super}_{\ell}. Taking i0i_{0} even larger, if necessary, assume that w⁡(i0)∉H⟂w(i_{0})\notin H^{\perp}, which is possible because w⁡(i)→w1∉H⟂w(i)\to w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}. (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is strongly w⁡(i0)w(i_{0})-endotactic, so there exists a w⁡(i0)w(i_{0})-sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} with x∈Superℓx\in\operatorname{Super}_{\ell}. Since (w⁡(i))(w(i)) is a unit jet adapted to (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), by definition x→x′x\to x^{\prime} is sustaining along the unit jet (w⁡(i))(w(i)). Proposition 6.20.1 implies that x→x′x\to x^{\prime} is w¯{\overline{w}}-sustaining. ∎

Remark 6.25.

Proposition 6.24 can be proven directly, using only Corollary 6.12.

Here is the main result of this section.

Example 6.27.

Proposition 6.26 is false without the assumption that w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}. For example, consider the network consisting of the single reversible reaction A⇌BA\rightleftharpoons B. The direction u=(1/2,1/2)u=(1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2}) is perpendicular to the stoichiometric subspace, and v=(−1/2,1/2)v=(-1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2}) lies in the subspace. Consider an adapted toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) framed by (u,v)(u,v). Then the reaction B→AB\to A is sustaining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)), while the reaction A→BA\to B is draining. The ratio of their pulls is

|pullB→A⁡(i)pullA→B⁡(i)|=θ​(i)⟨β1​(i)​u+β2​(i)​v,(0,1)−(1,0)⟩=(θ​(i)β2​(i))⟨v,(−1,1)⟩=(θ​(i)β2​(i))2.\displaystyle\bigg|\frac{\operatorname{pull}_{B\to A}(i)}{\operatorname{pull}_{A\to B}(i)}\bigg|=\theta(i)^{\langle\beta_{1}(i)u+\beta_{2}(i)v,~(0,1)-(1,0)\rangle}=(\theta(i)^{\beta_{2}(i)})^{\langle v,~(-1,1)\rangle}=(\theta(i)^{\beta_{2}(i)})^{\sqrt{2}}. (23)

In particular, if β2​(i)\beta_{2}(i) approaches 00 much faster than θ⁡(i)\theta(i) approaches ∞\infty, then the limit of θ​(i)β2​(i)\theta(i)^{\beta_{2}(i)} does not diverge, so the limit of the ratio (23) is not ∞\infty, whence the sustaining reaction does not dominate the draining reaction.

Remark 6.28.

The idea of using a sustaining reaction to dominate draining reactions in the proof of Proposition 6.26 is similar to arguments in the proof of Lemma 4.8 in the work of Anderson [4]. Furthermore, Anderson’s result is similar to our Theorem 7.5, below: essentially, both results show that a certain function decreases along trajectories outside a compact set. Anderson’s concept of “partitioning vectors y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C} along a sequence of trajectory points” focuses first on the question of which monomials θ⟨w,y⟩\theta^{\langle w,y\rangle} dominate, and then later in the analysis analyzes the inner product ⟨w,y′−y⟩\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle, whereas we consider the entire product θ⟨w,y⟩​⟨w,y′−y⟩\theta^{\langle w,y\rangle}\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle in the definition of pull (17). Anderson’s concept fits into ours in the following way. For a sequence of trajectory points, written as θ​(i)w⁡(i)\theta(i)^{w(i)}, that do not remain in a compact set, consider the “top tier” defined by the monomial or the pull, respectively. That is, the top tier is the set of reactions y→y′y\to y^{\prime} such that the corresponding monomials or, respectively, corresponding pulls dominate all others along the sequence. For strongly endotactic networks, these two top tiers coincide, with the possible exception of reactions orthogonal to a limiting direction of the vectors (w⁡(i))(w(i)).

Remark 6.29.

Some ideas in the proof of Proposition 6.26 are cognate to ideas in Power Geometry [12]. Specifically, in Power Geometry, to determine which terms in a polynomial dominate (for instance, when certain coordinates go to zero of infinity) one works in the log of the coordinates and examines which exponent vectors of the polynomial lie in the relevant face of the Newton polytope of the polynomial.

7 A Lyapunov-like function for strongly endotactic networks

This section uses the results on jets from the previous section to show (Theorem 7.5) that for strongly endotactic networks, outside a compact set the function g⁡(x)=∑i∈𝒮xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} from Definition 5.6 decreases along trajectories.

Definition 7.1.

If NN is a confined reaction system, specified by a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), a tempering κ\kappa, and an invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}, then gg decreases along trajectories of the mass-action differential inclusion (Definition 3.23) arising from NN outside a compact set if there exists a compact set 𝒦⊆int⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{K}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) such that for all trajectories x⁡(t)x(t), the time derivative satisfies dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))|t=t∗<0\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t))|_{t=t^{*}}<0 whenever x⁡(t∗)∈int⁡(𝒫)∖𝒦x(t^{*})\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\setminus\mathcal{K}.

Remark 7.2.

Every strict Lyapunov function decreases outside the compact set consisting of the function’s unique minimum. Functions that decrease outside a compact set should be compared with Foster–Lyapunov functions used in the analysis of Markov chains [32, Appendix B.1]. Foster–Lyapunov functions are used, for instance, to prove that a Markov chain always reaches a certain set, the analogue of our compact set 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

The next lemma states that our compact set of interest, 𝒦=𝒦θ\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_{\theta}, is a compact subset of the positive orthant ℝ>0𝒮\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}}. In contrast, some of the sublevel sets of the function gg are not compact. Indeed, it is the fact that some level sets of gg intersect the boundary of the positive orthant that prevents us from using the sublevel sets as our sets 𝒦\mathcal{K}; see Remark 8.10.

Lemma 7.3.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be an invariant polyhedron of a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), and let θ>1\theta>1. Then the set

𝒦θ={θ0w| 1≤θ0≤θ​ and ​w∈ℝ𝒮​ with ​‖w‖=1}∩𝒫\mathcal{K}_{\theta}=\big\{\theta_{0}^{w}\,\big|\,1\leq\theta_{0}\leq\theta\text{ and }w\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}\text{ with }||w||=1\big\}\cap\mathcal{P}

is a compact subset of int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}).

Proof.

𝒦θ\mathcal{K}_{\theta} is compact because it is the intersection of a closed set 𝒫\mathcal{P} with a continuous image (under coordinatewise exponential) of a compact set, namely, the closed ball of radius log⁡θ\log\theta around the origin in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}. The intersection is in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) because exponentials never vanish. ∎

Lemma 7.4.

Let NN be a confined reaction system, specified by a network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), a tempering κ\kappa, and an invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Suppose there exists θ>1\theta>1 such that

∑r=(y→y′)∈ℛkr​θ0⟨w,y⟩​⟨w,y′−y⟩<0\displaystyle\sum_{r=(y\to y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{R}}k_{r}\theta_{0}^{\langle w,y\rangle}\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0 (24)

for all θ0>θ\theta_{0}>\theta and unit vectors ww in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} with θ0w∈𝒫∖𝒦θ\theta_{0}^{w}\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\theta}, and for all (kr)r∈ℛ∈∏r∈ℛκ⁡(r)(k_{r})_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\in\prod_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa(r). Then outside the set 𝒦θ\mathcal{K}_{\theta} in Lemma 7.3, the function g⁡(x)=∑i∈𝒮xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} decreases along trajectories of the mass-action differential inclusion (Definition 3.23) arising from NN.

Proof.

We need dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))|t=t∗<0\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t))|_{t=t^{*}}<0 for any trajectory point x⁡(t∗)∈int⁡(𝒫)∖𝒦θx(t^{*})\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\theta}. Such a trajectory point can be written as x⁡(t∗)=θ0wx(t^{*})=\theta_{0}^{w} where θ0>θ\theta_{0}>\theta and ww is a unit vector in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}, by Lemma 7.3. Additionally, dd​t​x​(t)|t=t∗\frac{d}{dt}x(t)|_{t=t^{*}} has the form given in Definition 3.23 for some rates kr∈κ⁡(r)k_{r}\in\kappa(r). The following computation is straightforward, using of the gradient of gg:

dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))|t=t∗\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t))|_{t=t^{*}} =⟨∇g​(θ0w),∑r∈ℛkr​(θ0w)reactant⁡(r)​flux⁡(r)⟩\displaystyle=\Big\langle\nabla g(\theta_{0}^{w}),\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}k_{r}(\theta_{0}^{w})^{\operatorname{reactant}(r)}\operatorname{flux}(r)\Big\rangle
=⟨(log⁡θ0)​w,∑r∈ℛkr​θ0⟨w,reactant⁡(r)⟩​flux⁡(r)⟩\displaystyle=\Big\langle(\log\theta_{0})w,\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}k_{r}\theta_{0}^{\langle w,\operatorname{reactant}(r)\rangle}\operatorname{flux}(r)\Big\rangle
=(log⁡θ0)​∑r=(y→y′)∈ℛkr​θ0⟨w,y⟩​⟨w,y′−y⟩.\displaystyle=(\log\theta_{0})\sum_{r=(y\to y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{R}}k_{r}\theta_{0}^{\langle w,y\rangle}\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle.

As log⁡θ0>0\log\theta_{0}>0 because θ0>1\theta_{0}>1, the desired inequality dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))|t=t∗<0\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t))|_{t=t^{*}}<0 follows from (24). ∎

Theorem 7.5.

If NN is a confined strongly endotactic reaction system, specified by a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), a tempering κ\kappa, and an invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}, then outside a compact set 𝒦⊆ℝ>0𝒮\mathcal{K}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}_{>0}, the function g⁡(x)=∑i∈𝒮xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} decreases along trajectories of the mass-action differential inclusion (Definition 3.23) arising from NN.

Proof.

Begin by fixing a number 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 such that ε\varepsilon is a lower bound for the tempering κ\kappa and 1/ε1/\varepsilon is an upper bound: for all reactions r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, κ⁡(r)⊆(ε,1/ε)\kappa(r)\subseteq(\varepsilon,1/\varepsilon). The goal is to demonstrate the existence of a cutoff θ>1\theta>1 such that gg decreases along trajectories outside of the compact subset 𝒦θ⊆int⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{K}_{\theta}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) from Lemma 7.3. The proof proceeds by contradiction: assuming that no such θ\theta exists, construct an impossible toric jet.

To be precise, assume g⁡(x)g(x) fails to decrease along trajectories outside of each set 𝒦θ\mathcal{K}_{\theta}. Pick a sequence θ⁡(i)→∞\theta(i)\to\infty of real numbers >1>1, so 𝒦θ⁡(1)⊆𝒦θ⁡(2)⊆⋯\mathcal{K}_{\theta(1)}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{\theta(2)}\subseteq\cdots and ⋃i𝒦θ⁡(i)=ℝ>0𝒮\bigcup_{i}\mathcal{K}_{\theta(i)}=\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}}. Lemma 7.4 grants

  • ∙\bullet

    a sequence of points x⁡(i)=θ​(i)w⁡(i)∈𝒫x(i)=\theta(i)^{w(i)}\in\mathcal{P}, where w⁡(i)w(i) is a unit vector in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}, and

  • ∙\bullet

    for each reaction r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, a sequence kr​(i)k_{r}(i) of rates in the interval κ⁡(r)\kappa(r)

such that for all ii,

∑r=(y→y′)∈ℛkr​(i)​θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),y⟩​⟨w⁡(i),y′−y⟩≥0.\sum_{r=(y\to y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{R}}k_{r}(i)\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),y\rangle}\langle w(i),y^{\prime}-y\rangle\geq 0. (25)

Lemma 6.7 produces a subsequence of (w⁡(i))(w(i)) that is a unit jet; call its jet frame (w1,…,wℓ)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{\ell}) in ℝ𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}} and, as usual, denote the subsequence again by (w⁡(i))(w(i)), for ease of notation. The resulting sequence (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) is a toric jet by construction. Lemma 6.7 affords a subsequence that is adapted to (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), and it is this toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) whose impossibility we demonstrate by appeal to Proposition 6.26, which leverages the strongly endotactic hypothesis on (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) to deduce the opposite of the inequality (25).

Both kr​(i)k_{r}(i) and θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),y⟩\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),y\rangle} in (25) remain strictly positive. The only negative contributions to the sum in (25) are from reactions that are sustaining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)), whereas draining reactions contribute positively. To contradict (25), it suffices to show that for any reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} that is draining along (w⁡(i))(w(i)), the contribution to the sum (25) of some sustaining reaction x→x′x\to x^{\prime} eventually dominates that of y→y′y\to y^{\prime} by at least a factor of |ℛ||\mathcal{R}|, the number of reactions of the network. In other words, for a fixed draining reaction r=(y→y′)r=(y\to y^{\prime}), it suffices to exhibit a sustaining reaction rsus=(x→x′)r_{\mathrm{sus}}=(x\to x^{\prime}) such that the inequality

krsus​(i)kr​(i)​θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩​⟨w⁡(i),x′−x⟩⟨w⁡(i),y−y′⟩>|ℛ|\displaystyle\frac{k_{r_{\mathrm{sus}}}(i)}{k_{r}(i)}\theta(i)^{\langle w(i),x-y\rangle}\frac{\langle w(i),x^{\prime}-x\rangle}{\langle w(i),y-y^{\prime}\rangle}\ >\ |\mathcal{R}| (26)

holds for large ii. The number ε\varepsilon was constructed early in the proof so that krsus​(i)>εk_{r_{\mathrm{sus}}}(i)>\varepsilon and kr​(i)<1/εk_{r}(i)<1/\varepsilon. Consequently, the desired inequality (26) follows from the inequality

|pullx→x′⁡(i)pully→y′⁡(i)|=θ​(i)⟨w⁡(i),x−y⟩​⟨w⁡(i),x′−x⟩⟨w⁡(i),y−y′⟩>|ℛ|ε2.\left\lvert\frac{\operatorname{pull}_{x\to x^{\prime}}(i)}{\operatorname{pull}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(i)}\right\rvert\ =\ \theta(i)^{\langle w(i),~x-y\rangle}~\frac{\langle w(i),x^{\prime}-x\rangle}{\langle w(i),y-y^{\prime}\rangle}\ >\ \frac{|\mathcal{R}|}{\varepsilon^{2}}.

It is sufficient (but not necessary) to prove that the left-hand side of this inequality has limit ∞\infty, i.e., the draining reaction is dominated by some sustaining reaction along this adapted toric jet. This follows from Proposition 6.26, completing the proof, once w1w_{1} is verified not to be orthogonal to the stoichiometric subspace HH.

To prove that w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}, first express each vector wjw_{j} of the jet frame uniquely as a sum wj,H+wj,H⟂w_{j,H}+w_{j,H^{\perp}} of a vector wj,H∈Hw_{j,H}\in H and a vector wj,H⟂∈H⟂w_{j,H^{\perp}}\in H^{\perp}. Birch’s theorem (Theorem 5.12) produces a unique point qq in the intersection int⁡(𝒫)∩{θw∣θ∈ℝ>0​ and ​w∈H⟂}\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\cap\{\theta^{w}\mid\theta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\text{ and }w\in\nolinebreak H^{\perp}\}. Pick a neighborhood 𝒪\mathcal{O} in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) around qq whose closure 𝒪¯{\overline{\mathcal{O}}} is also contained in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}). The sequence (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big) eventually avoids 𝒪\mathcal{O}, because x⁡(i)x(i) approaches the boundary of the closure 𝒫¯{\overline{\mathcal{P}}} of 𝒫\mathcal{P} in the compactification [0,∞]𝒮[0,\infty]^{\mathcal{S}} (see Remark 6.3). Thus, by Corollary 5.18, there exists a number 0<μ≤10<\mu\leq 1 such that the HH-components wH​(i)w_{H}(i) of the unit vectors w⁡(i)w(i) have norm at least μ\mu, for large ii:

∥wH​(i)∥=∥β1​(i)​w1,H+⋯+βℓ​(i)​wℓ,H∥≥μ.\lVert w_{H}(i)\rVert=\lVert\beta_{1}({i})w_{1,H}+\cdots+\beta_{\ell}({i})w_{\ell,H}\rVert\geq\mu.

Since the first coefficient β1​(i)\beta_{1}({i}) approaches 11 while all others approach 00, the left-hand side of this inequality has limit ∥w1,H∥\lVert w_{1,H}\rVert, so ∥w1,H∥≥μ>0\lVert w_{1,H}\rVert\geq\mu>0. Thus w1,H≠0w_{1,H}\neq 0, as desired. ∎

Remark 7.6.

We wish to emphasize that our extensions of Birch’s Theorem (in particular, Corollary 5.18) were used in the proof of Theorem 7.5 to show that w1∉H⟂w_{1}\notin H^{\perp}. This novel use of Birch’s Theorem is one of our main contributions.

8 Main results: persistence and permanence

In this section, we prove that strongly endotactic networks have bounded trajectories (Theorem 8.1), are persistent (Theorem 8.5), and are permanent (Theorem 1.1). Although the permanence result is stronger than the first two, the two weaker results are applied in the proof of permanence. In this section, we rely on two key prior results:

  • ∙\bullet

    the decrease of the pseudo-Helmholtz free energy function along trajectories outside a compact set (Theorem 7.5), and

  • ∙\bullet

    a projection argument from our earlier work [24].

Additionally, we prove the existence of steady states for strongly endotactic networks in the mass-action ODE setting.

Throughout this section, Notation 5.1 remains in effect, as does Definition 5.6, which includes the special case g⁡(x)=g(1,…,1)​(x)=∑i=1|𝒮|xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=g_{(1,\ldots,1)}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} from [19, 26, 27].

8.1 Boundedness of trajectories

Conjecture 4.7 holds for strongly endotactic networks.

Theorem 8.1.

Strongly endotactic networks have bounded trajectories. More precisely, the image of every trajectory of every mass-action differential inclusion (Definition 3.23) arising from a confined strongly endotactic reaction system is bounded.

Proof.

For a mass-action differential inclusion of a confined strongly endotactic reaction system, specified by (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), a tempering κ\kappa, and an invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}, let x:I→int⁡(𝒫)x:I\to\nolinebreak\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) denote a trajectory. By Theorem 7.5, there exists a compact set 𝒦⊆int⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{K}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) such that dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))|t=t∗<0\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t))|_{t=t^{*}}<0 for all trajectory points x⁡(t∗)∈int⁡(𝒫)∖𝒦x(t^{*})\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P})\setminus\mathcal{K}. Let M1=sup{g⁡(x)∣x∈𝒦}M_{1}=\sup\{g(x)\mid x\in\mathcal{K}\} be the supremum of gg on 𝒦\mathcal{K}, which is finite by compactness. Let MM be the maximum of M1M_{1} and g⁡(infI)g(\inf I). Then x⁡(t)x(t) remains in the bounded sublevel set 𝒬={x∈𝒫∣g⁡(x)≤M}\mathcal{Q}=\{x\in\mathcal{P}\mid g(x)\leq M\}. Indeed, the trajectory begins in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} by construction; when it is in 𝒬∖𝒦\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathcal{K}, the value of gg decreases; and while it is in 𝒦\mathcal{K}, the value of gg can not exceed M1M_{1} and thus can not exceed MM. ∎

8.2 Persistence

Our next main result is the persistence of strongly endotactic networks (Theorem 8.5). The proof appeals to the following lemma, a special case of [3, Theorem 3.7] of Anderson or [13, Proposition 20] of Craciun et al. It again concerns the function g⁡(x)=∑i=1mxi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i}, which extends continuously to the boundary of the nonnegative orthant.

Lemma 8.2.

The function g⁡(x)=∑i=1mxi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} defined on ℝ≥0m\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m} has a local maximum at the origin.

Another result crucial to our proof of Theorem 8.5 is the next lemma, which follows from our earlier work on “vertexical” families of differential inclusions on hypercubes that are well-behaved under maps [24].

Lemma 8.3.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the class of all confined strongly endotactic reaction systems. If

  1. 1.

    every mass-action differential inclusion of every reaction system in ℱ\mathcal{F} is repelled by the origin (Definition 4.1), and

  2. 2.

    every trajectory of such a differential inclusion is bounded,

then every strongly endotactic reaction network is persistent.

Proof.

This is a special case of Corollary 6.4 of [24]. ∎

To be useful, Lemma 8.3 requires the following auxiliary result.

Lemma 8.4.

If the function g⁡(x)=∑i∈𝒮xi​log⁡xi−xig(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_{i}\log x_{i}-x_{i} for a confined reaction system NN decreases along trajectories outside a compact set, then the mass-action differential inclusion (Definition 3.23) arising from NN is repelled by the origin.

Proof.

Let O1O_{1} be a relatively open neighborhood of the origin 0¯∈ℝ≥0𝒮{\overline{0}}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{S}}, and let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be an invariant polyhedron of (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}). Let 𝒦⊆int⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{K}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) denote a compact set outside of which gg decreases along trajectories. If 𝒫\mathcal{P} does not contain 0¯{\overline{0}}, then all trajectories avoid a fixed neighborhood of the origin because they remain in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Therefore assume 𝒫\mathcal{P} contains 0¯{\overline{0}}. Let NεN_{\varepsilon} denote the intersection of the nonnegative orthant ℝ≥0𝒮\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{S}} with an open ball of radius ε\varepsilon around the origin. Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be sufficiently small so that

  • ∙\bullet

    O1O_{1} contains NεN_{\varepsilon},

  • ∙\bullet

    ε\varepsilon is less than the distance between the origin 0¯{\overline{0}} and the compact set 𝒦\mathcal{K}, and

  • ∙\bullet

    the maximum of gg on NεN_{\varepsilon} is attained uniquely at the origin (cf. Lemma 8.2).

As g⁡(0¯)=0g({\overline{0}})=0, it follows that gg is strictly negative on NεN_{\varepsilon}. Define −M-M to be the maximum value of gg for nonnegative vectors of norm ε\varepsilon, which is attained by compactness:

−M=max⁡{g⁡(z)|z∈ℝ≥0𝒮​ with ​∥z∥=ε}.\displaystyle-M=\max\big\{g(z)\,\big|\,z\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{S}}\text{ with }\lVert z\rVert=\varepsilon\big\}. (27)

Thus, −M<g⁡(0¯)=0-M<g({\overline{0}})=0. Again by Lemma 8.2, there exists δ>0\delta>0 so that g(z)>−M/2g(z)>-M/2 for z∈Nδz\in N_{\delta}. It is enough to show that any trajectory x:I→int⁡(𝒫)x:I\to\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) that begins outside O1O_{1}, and thus outside NεN_{\varepsilon} as well, never enters NδN_{\delta}. Indeed, if the trajectory ever enters the closure of NεN_{\varepsilon} at some point x⁡(t∗)x(t^{*}), then g⁡(x⁡(t∗))≤−Mg(x(t^{*}))\leq-M by (27). Thus, since g⁡(x⁡(t))g(x(t)) decreases while x⁡(t)x(t) is in NεN_{\varepsilon}, because Nε∩𝒦N_{\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal{K} is empty, x⁡(t)x(t) never reaches NδN_{\delta} by definition of δ\delta. ∎

We can now prove that Conjecture 4.4 holds for strongly endotactic networks networks.

Theorem 8.5.

Strongly endotactic networks are persistent.

Proof.

Follows from Lemmas 8.3 and 8.4 and Theorems 7.5 and 8.1. ∎

In addition, the GAC holds for strongly endotactic complex-balanced systems.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Use Theorem 8.5 and the discussion before Conjecture 4.4. ∎

Remark 8.6.

Our reliance on the projection argument (Lemma 8.3) requires showing that for strongly endotactic networks, the origin is repelling and trajectories are bounded. Instead of Lemma 8.3, we could have appealed to a related result, Corollary 6.3 in [24], which states that for a “vertexical” family of differential inclusions—such as the family arising from strongly endotactic networks—if all vertices of [0,∞]𝒮[0,\infty]^{\mathcal{S}} are repelling, then the boundary of [0,∞]𝒮[0,\infty]^{\mathcal{S}} is repelling and hence these networks are persistent. However, it is not known whether non-origin vertices of [0,∞]𝒮[0,\infty]^{\mathcal{S}} are repelling for strongly endotactic networks.

8.3 Permanence

Lemma 8.3 only records half of Corollary 6.4 of [24]. The other half deals with permanence.

Lemma 8.7.

In Lemma 8.3, assume that 1 and 2 hold, and that XX is such a differential inclusion on ℝ>0𝒮\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}}. If K⊆ℝ>0𝒮K\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}} is a compact set for which there exists A∈ℝ>0A\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} such that every trajectory of XX that starts in KK remains bounded above by AA in each coordinate for all time, then for some compact set K+⊆ℝ>0𝒮K^{+}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}}, no trajectory of XX that begins in KK leaves K+K^{+}.

Applying Lemma 8.7 requires an auxiliary result that makes use of the persistence result.

Lemma 8.8.

Let XX be the mass-action differential inclusion of a confined strongly endotactic reaction system NN, specified by a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) together with a tempering κ\kappa and an invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Then there exists a compact set KK in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) such that the image of every trajectory of XX defined on a ray meets KK.

Proof.

By Theorem 7.5, there exists a compact set 𝒦⊆int⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{K}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) outside of which gg decreases along trajectories. Enlarge 𝒦\mathcal{K} to a closed ε\varepsilon-neighborhood of 𝒦\mathcal{K}, denoted by 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}, so that 𝒦~⊆int⁡(𝒫)\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}); thus 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}} is compact. Let x:I→int⁡(𝒫)x:I\to\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) be a trajectory of the mass-action differential inclusion arising from (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) with κ\kappa and 𝒫\mathcal{P}, where I=[a,∞]I=[a,\infty] is a ray. The goal is to show that the image of xx meets 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}. If x⁡(a)∈𝒦~x(a)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}, then we are done. Otherwise, there exists a nonempty maximal subinterval [a,b)⊂I[a,b)\subset I on which g⁡(x⁡(t))g(x(t)) is decreasing. If b<∞b<\infty, then x⁡(b)∈𝒦x(b)\in\mathcal{K}, so we are done. The remaining case has g⁡(x⁡(t))g(x(t)) decreasing for all time t>at>a. The closure of the trajectory x⁡(t)x(t) is a compact subset of int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}), because this network has bounded trajectories (Theorem 8.1) and is persistent (Theorem 8.5).

Any trajectory x⁡(t)x(t) that fails to intersect 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}} is bounded away from 𝒦\mathcal{K}. The time derivative dd​t​g​(x⁡(t))\frac{d}{dt}g(x(t)) of such a trajectory is therefore negative and bounded away from 00 (otherwise the closure of the trajectory would meet 𝒦\mathcal{K}, forcing the trajectory itself to meet 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}), causing g⁡(x⁡(t))g(x(t)) to have limit −∞-\infty as t→∞t\to\infty. But gg is bounded below by −|𝒮|-|\mathcal{S}|, so we conclude that every trajectory x⁡(t)x(t) must visit the compact set 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}. ∎

We now prove our main result, which states that strongly endotactic networks are permanent, thereby resolving Conjecture 4.5 in the strongly endotactic case.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

First, strongly endotactic networks are persistent by Theorem 8.5. Next, by Lemma 8.8, for every mass-action differential inclusion XX arising from a strongly endotactic network, there exists a compact set KK in the positive orthant that meets every trajectory of XX defined on a ray. For the purpose of studying eventual properties of trajectories such as permanence, we therefore assume that each trajectory defined on a ray begins in KK. Lemma 8.7 applies for strongly endotactic networks by Lemma 8.4 along with Theorems 7.5 and 8.1; it implies that there exists a compact set K+K^{+} in ℝ>0𝒮\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}} such that every such trajectory eventually remains in K+K^{+}. Thus XX is permanent. ∎

As a corollary, certain weakly reversible networks are permanent.

Corollary 8.9.

If each linkage class of a weakly reversible network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) has the same stoichiometric subspace, namely that of (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), then (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is permanent.

Proof.

Follows from Corollary 3.19 and Theorem 1.1. ∎

Similarly, weakly reversible reaction networks with one linkage class are permanent.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Follows from the Corollary 3.20 and Theorem 1.1. ∎

Remark 8.10.

Is an appeal to our earlier work (Lemmas 8.3 and 8.7) necessary to prove permanence? Could the fact that gg decreases along trajectories suffice to deduce Theorem 1.1? Such an approach seems not to work. On one hand, we can prove that maximal trajectories must approach a prescribed compact set in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, namely the smallest sublevel set QQ of gg that contains 𝒦\mathcal{K}. On the other hand, QQ may meet the boundary of 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Thus the union of all ω\omega-limit sets of all possible trajectories lies in Q∩int⁡(𝒫)Q\cap\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}), but its closure in 𝒫\mathcal{P} could meet the boundary of int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}). Another approach to permanence is to determine whether 𝒦\mathcal{K} is an attracting set. However, this also seems not to work: although persistence can be used to prove that every trajectory outside 𝒦\mathcal{K} must enter a neighborhood of 𝒦\mathcal{K} (denoted by 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}} in the proof of Lemma 8.8), the trajectory could exit and re-enter 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}} infinitely often.

8.4 Existence of positive steady states

In the setting of mass-action ODE systems, Deng et al. proved that for weakly reversible networks, each invariant polyhedron contains a positive steady state [16]. As for two-dimensional endotactic networks, Craciun, Nazarov, and Pantea [15, §6] explained that their permanence result, together with the Brouwer fixed-point theorem [36, §55], implies the existence of positive steady states. (Their result is complementary to that of Deng et al., because weakly reversible networks form a proper subset of endotactic networks.) This standard application of the Brouwer fixed-point theorem to establish the existence of positive steady states in the setting of reaction systems goes back at least to Wei in 1962 [50].

We too are able to prove the existence of positive steady states (Corollary 8.12). However, this is not accomplished via the Brouwer fixed-point theorem, because we do not readily obtain a forward-invariant set UU in ℝ>0𝒮\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{S}} that is homeomorphic to a ball; in particular, the sets KK and K+K^{+} in the proofs of Lemma 8.8 and Theorem 1.1 do not suffice. Instead our proof relies on the following result concerning fixed points of dynamical systems, a special case of [42, Theorem 3] first proven in a general setting by Srzednicki [48].

Lemma 8.11.

Let XX be a continuous ODE system on a polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that every trajectory of XX defined on a ray meets a compact set KK. Then XX has a steady state.

Corollary 8.12.

For a mass-action kinetics ODE system arising from a strongly endotactic network, each invariant polyhedron contains a positive steady state.

Proof.

Let XX denote such a mass-action kinetics ODE system with invariant polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The proof of Lemma 8.8 shows that there exists a compact set KK in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}) such that the image of every trajectory of XX defined on a ray meets KK. Thus, by Lemma 8.11, XX has a steady state in KK, which is therefore in int⁡(𝒫)\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{P}). ∎

9 Examples

The examples here illustrate our results as well as their limitations.

9.1 Strongly endotactic networks

Example 9.1.

By Theorem 1.1, the strongly endotactic network from Example 3.16, comprised of the reactions 0→3​A+B0\to 3A+B, 2​A→B2A\to B, and 2​B→A+B2B\to A+B, is permanent.

Permanence of the network in Example 9.1 already was known by the results of Craciun, Nazarov, and Pantea [15] and extensions by Pantea [39], which apply to endotactic networks with stoichiometric subspace of dimension at most 22. For the following 33-dimensional example, their results do not apply.

Example 9.2.

The following network is strongly endotactic, so it is permanent:

0→A→B→C→0.0\to A\to B\to C\to 0.

The weaker persistence result for the network in Example 9.2 follows from work of Angeli, De Leenheer, and Sontag [9] because it has no siphons. In contrast, the following example contains critical siphons, so the results of Angeli, De Leenheer, and Sontag do not apply.

Example 9.3.

The following network is strongly endotactic, so it is permanent:

2​A⇌B2​B⇌C2​C⇌A.2A\rightleftharpoons B\quad\quad 2B\rightleftharpoons C\quad\quad 2C\rightleftharpoons A.

Combinatorially, the reactant polytope is a triangular prism; one triangle is formed by AA, BB, and CC, and the other is formed by 2​A2A, 2​B2B, and 2​C2C. Each of the three pairs of reversible reactions lies along a diagonal of one of the quadrilateral boundary faces of the polytope.

Persistence in Example 9.3 already was known by work of Johnston and Siegel [29], which extends easily to the setting of mass-action differential inclusions, because the unique critical siphon {A,B,C}\{A,B,C\} can be shown to be weakly dynamically non-emptiable. In the next example, however, no previous results apply to obtain persistence: it is a three-dimensional network for which {A,B,C}\{A,B,C\} is a critical siphon but not weakly dynamically non-emptiable.

Example 9.4.

The following network is strongly endotactic and therefore permanent:

4​A→A+B+C→4​B→4​C→2​A+2​C.4A\to A+B+C\to 4B\to 4C\to 2A+2C.

The reactant polytope is a tetrahedron with vertices A+B+CA+B+C, 4​A4A, 4​B4B, and 4​C4C. Each of the four reactions lies on or is a subset of one of the six edges of the tetrahedron.

9.2 Limitations of the geometric approach

The geometric approach presented in this work has some limitations in its ability to resolve Conjectures 4.3–4.7 in full generality. We explain these limitations via a simple example.

Example 9.5.

The following network GG is endotactic but not strongly endotactic:

0⇌AB⇌2​B.0\rightleftharpoons A\quad\quad B\rightleftharpoons 2B.

Define a toric jet adapted to GG in the following way: take any sequence (θ⁡(i))(\theta(i)) of numbers greater than 1 that limits to infinity, and let w(i)=−(1θ⁡(i),1)/∥(1θ⁡(i),1)∥w(i)=-(\frac{1}{\theta(i)},1)/\lVert(\frac{1}{\theta(i)},1)\rVert. It is straightforward to verify that the conclusion of Proposition 6.26 fails for every subsequence of the resulting toric jet (θ​(i)w⁡(i))\big(\theta(i)^{w(i)}\big). Namely, the pull of the draining reaction 0←A0\leftarrow A with respect to the toric jet cannot be dominated by either of the two sustaining reactions 0→A0\to A or B→2​BB\to 2B. Although results of Craciun, Nazarov, and Pantea [15, 39] can prove that this two-dimensional system is permanent, higher-dimensional generalizations of this network can not be proved to be permanent or even persistent.

The limiting direction of the unit jet here is limn→∞w⁡(n)=(0,−1)\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}w(n)=(0,-1), and this direction (0,−1)(0,-1) witnesses the fact that the network fails to be strongly endotactic. Namely, there is no reaction with reactant among the ≤(0,−1)\leq_{(0,-1)}-maximal reactants {0,A}\{0,A\} and product outside of that set. Our results for strongly endotactic networks rely on the existence of such a sustaining reaction, so they are unable to prove permanence or even persistence of this network or similar networks by way of toric jets.

In our final example, the question of persistence is as yet unresolved.

Example 9.6.

The following 33-dimensional network is weakly reversible—and therefore endotactic—but not strongly endotactic:

A→B→C→A2​A⇌3​B.A\to B\to C\to A\quad\quad 2A\rightleftharpoons 3B.

The reactant polytope is a pyramid whose base has vertices AA, 2​A2A, BB, and 3​B3B. Three of the reactions form a triangle along edges of the pyramid, while the remaining pair of reversible reactions lies on the edge of the pyramid nonadjacent to the triangle. The network has a unique critical siphon, {A,B,C}\{A,B,C\}, which is not weakly dynamically non-emptiable. Persistence and permanence (Conjectures 4.4 and 4.5) remain open for this network.
